analysis.one_liner: Boosts unpaid wages, severance, and retiree benefits in business bankruptcies and restricts executive bonuses there.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a single vote: introduced in January 2015, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee twelve days later, and never heard from again before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite bankruptcy rules when a company goes broke. Workers' unpaid wages and pension contributions would rank higher in the payoff line, severance would be paid in full, and unions could file claims on behalf of employees. Companies would need a judge's sign-off, with strong proof, before tearing up union contracts or cutting retiree health benefits, and courts would have to weigh whether a bidder keeps jobs before approving a sale. At the same time, it would clamp down on the bonuses and golden parachutes executives of bankrupt companies often collect while workers absorb cuts.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees and retirees of companies that file for bankruptcy: they would recover up to $20,000 in unpaid wages and benefit contributions with higher priority, get severance treated as fully earned, keep retiree health benefits unless a judge finds deep cuts are truly necessary, and gain claims for pension and company-stock losses when the employer committed fraud. Unions would gain standing to file claims and bargain in bankruptcy. Bankruptcy judges would favor bidders who preserve jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Raises the priority cap for unpaid wages, salaries, and commissions in bankruptcy from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker, and raises the benefit-plan priority from $10,000 to $20,000 per covered employee.
Treats severance pay owed to laid-off workers as an administrative expense of the bankruptcy estate, deemed earned in full, giving it near-top repayment priority.

Makes a company's retiree health benefits continue at their pre-filing level unless the debtor negotiates reductions in good faith and a judge finds, on clear and convincing evidence, that the cuts are the minimum needed for the company to survive.

Allows bankruptcy courts to approve a sale of business assets only after weighing whether the bidder will keep existing jobs, preserve wages and conditions, and take on pension and retiree health obligations.

Bars approval of plan payments to insiders, senior executives, and the 20 next most highly paid employees unless they are part of a program shared with the nonmanagement workforce and not disproportionate to it, and lets courts claw back executive pay in proportion to cuts imposed on workers and retirees.
Lets unions file proofs of claim for their members and lets grievance and arbitration proceedings under union contracts continue despite the bankruptcy filing.

analysis.who_pays: Executives, consultants, and other insiders of bankrupt companies would lose access to retention bonuses, enhanced compensation, and deferred-compensation packages while their workforce absorbs cuts, and could face clawbacks. Secured lenders and buyers of distressed companies would face higher claims ahead of them in line and could recover less from collateral. Distressed-debt investors could pay more to acquire companies, since keeping jobs and benefits counts toward the best offer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives, consultants, and lenders in bankrupt firms

drawbacks.text: Higher repayment priority for wage, severance, and benefit claims would leave less for secured lenders and other creditors, which could make bankruptcy financing more expensive or harder to obtain, raising costs for distressed companies generally.

Making it substantially harder to reject a collective bargaining agreement could, in some cases, push a failing company toward outright liquidation rather than a leaner reorganization, costing all jobs instead of preserving most of them at reduced terms; the bill's own standard aims to prevent this, but the trade-off is real.
The bar of clear and convincing evidence for cutting union contracts and retiree benefits would give debtors less flexibility than current law, adding litigation time and cost to Chapter 11 cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, recurring harm: in large bankruptcies, workers and retirees have repeatedly absorbed benefit cuts and unpaid wages while management collected retention bonuses and severance. The main cost falls on executives of distressed firms and on creditors, who would move down the repayment line. The credible downside is that tighter limits on tearing up union contracts could occasionally tip a borderline company from reorganization into liquidation, which would hurt the same workers the bill protects; the bill's minimum-savings standard tries to guard against that, but the risk is genuine rather than imaginary.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law subcommittee, got no hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on January 6, 2015 with six Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law on January 12, 2015.
No further action appears in the record: the subcommittee and full committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives, consultants, and lenders at bankrupt companies kept the existing rules, which let firms shed union contracts and retiree health benefits in bankruptcy without the added proof requirements, and continue collecting retention bonuses and deferred compensation that this bill would have curtailed. Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies remain on the weaker footing the bill would have lifted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bankrupt firms' executives and their lenders

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call splits exist, but its support was entirely one-party.

industries.industry: Executives and consultants of bankrupt companies
industries.note: The bill would bar court approval of retention bonuses, enhanced compensation, and deferred-compensation packages for insiders and top executives unless they mirror a program shared with the rank-and-file, and would claw back executive pay in proportion to cuts imposed on workers and retirees. Under current rules, management compensation in bankruptcy faces much lighter scrutiny while employees absorb the cuts.

Unpaid wages, severance, and benefits for postpetition work would become charges against lenders' collateral even where the trustee waived such claims, and higher worker priorities would leave lenders with less. Buyers of distressed assets would have to offer job and benefit preservation to win the 'best bid.'

Unions would gain standing to file creditor claims for members, guaranteed fee reimbursement in contract-rejection fights, and a much heavier burden on debtors seeking to reject collective bargaining agreements or cut retiree health benefits, with any cuts limited to the minimum the company needs to survive.
